claims.text: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloys have a coarse, possibly strained, single-phase hexagonal structure comparable to arc-melted or melt-spun forms.
Argon–nitrogen annealing combined with cyclic longitudinal tensile straining reduces residual internal stress.
Argon–nitrogen annealing combined with cyclic longitudinal tensile straining refines grain-boundary structures.
Reduced residual stress and refined grain boundaries promote more homogeneous nucleation of the magnetostructural transition.
More uniformly distributed nucleation and growth make the first-order magnetostructural transition less abrupt.
Making the magnetostructural transition less abrupt reduces magnetic hysteresis.
The treated alloy will retain a significant magnetic entropy change despite the less abrupt transition.
Treated samples will have narrower hysteresis loops than untreated as-deposited controls during low-field cycling.
Treated samples will show a smoother and possibly slightly moderated magnetocaloric entropy-change profile relative to untreated controls.
Untreated as-deposited alloys exhibit a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition with significant hysteresis.
Untreated as-deposited alloys have limited heat-exchange rates because of coarse microstructure and inherent residual stress.

The proposed intervention will be effective across non-equiatomic compositions within the FeMnNiGeSi family made as nanostructured forms by methods such as magnetron co-sputtering or electron-beam lithography.
The magnitudes of the hysteresis and entropy-change responses depend sensitively on annealing parameters, strain-cycle amplitude, and sample geometry.
Comparing treated samples with untreated as-deposited controls under the same low-field cycles can test the proposed microstructure-mediated mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis identifies annealing plus cyclic tensile straining as the controlled intervention, whereas the intervention field also offers fabrication of nanoribbon-like structures by electron-beam lithography as an alternative. These are materially different interventions, so the experiment is not consistently defined as one controlled intervention.
